details:
**The World as Will and Representation**
Schopenhauer's magnum opus (first published 1818/1819, also translated as The World as Will and Idea) and the near-universal giveaway. It argues that the world as we experience it is mere representation, while the underlying reality is a single blind, striving Will, and its four books cover epistemology, metaphysics of nature, aesthetics, and ethics.

**"Will to life" and its negation**
Schopenhauer's term (Wille zum Leben) for the blind, ceaseless striving that drives all living things and causes endless suffering. He argued that salvation lies in denying or negating the will to life through asceticism and resignation.

**Pessimism**
Schopenhauer is the archetypal "pessimistic" philosopher, holding that life is fundamentally suffering because desire can never be permanently satisfied. Nearly every question calls him a pessimist in its giveaway.

**Kant and the "thing-in-itself"**
Schopenhauer saw himself as Kant's true heir. He identified Kant's unknowable "thing-in-itself" (noumenon) with the Will, which we know directly through our own bodies, and our body is both will from the inside and representation from the outside. His magnum opus includes an appendix, "Critique of the Kantian Philosophy."

**Aesthetics as escape and the supremacy of music**
In the third book of his magnum opus, Schopenhauer argues that aesthetic contemplation gives a temporary escape from the suffering of willing. Music is the highest art because it is not a copy of the Ideas but a direct copy of the Will itself, a view that deeply inspired Richard Wagner.

**Upanishads, Vedas, and Buddhism**
Schopenhauer was one of the first Western philosophers to draw heavily on Indian thought, quoting the Upanishads and comparing his ideas to Buddhism. He based his ethics of compassion on the Sanskrit phrase "tat tvam asi" ("thou art that"), meaning that the self and others are ultimately one.

**On the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason**
Schopenhauer's 1813 doctoral dissertation. It divides the principle of sufficient reason (adopted from Leibniz) into four forms governing becoming (fiendi), knowing (cognoscendi), being (essendi), and acting (agendi). In it he mocks the ontological argument for God as a "charming joke."

**"Schopenhauer as Educator"**
The third of Friedrich Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations. Nietzsche praises Schopenhauer's honesty, cheerfulness, and steadfastness as a model for renewing German culture, contrasting him with figures like David Strauss, and it contains the line "There is in the world one road whereon none may go, except thou."

**On the Basis of Morality and compassion (Mitleid)**
A prize essay arguing that compassion, not Kantian duty, is the foundation of morality. It names egoism, malice, and compassion as the three basic incentives of human action. The Royal Danish Society of Sciences declined to award it its prize even though it was the only entry.

**The Art of Being Right**
A satirical treatise (also called The Art of Controversy) listing 38 stratagems for winning arguments regardless of truth. The final stratagem is to "become personal, insulting, and rude" when your opponent is winning, that is, an ad hominem attack.

**"On Women"**
A notoriously misogynistic essay from Schopenhauer's collection Parerga and Paralipomena (Greek for "additions and omissions"). It claims women are not meant for much mental or physical work and cannot take a purely objective interest in anything.

**Animals and poodles**
Schopenhauer loved his pet poodles and argued strongly for compassion toward animals. He criticized thinkers like Spinoza and Kant for treating animals as mere means for human use, and held that cruelty to animals shows a lack of goodness.

**On Vision and Colors**
A treatise on color theory written after discussions with Goethe, whose own theory of colors Schopenhauer partly adopted and partly corrected. He later sent the work to Charles Locke Eastlake, the English translator of Goethe's Theory of Colours, explaining his views on how the retina produces color.

**Rivalry with Hegel**
As a lecturer at the University of Berlin, Schopenhauer deliberately scheduled his lectures at the same time as Hegel's. Almost no students came, and his academic career failed; he despised Hegel for the rest of his life.

**On the Freedom of the Will**
Another prize essay, in which Schopenhauer denies free will, arguing that every action follows necessarily from a sufficient motive acting on a person's fixed character. It was published together with On the Basis of Morality as The Two Fundamental Problems of Ethics.
